lead: This unit explains how a web request travels from a URL, through DNS and HTTP, to a browser and server, and back as a page or API response. You learn the architecture and roles behind a full stack app, then use the same tools a developer uses to inspect, version and debug it.
about: Chapter 1.1 starts with the Internet, the World Wide Web and DNS, following a URL to an IP address. Chapter 1.2 turns that path into client-server and multi-tier architecture. Chapter 1.3 names the parts: browsers, web servers and application servers. Chapter 1.4 makes the request concrete with HTTP and HTTPS, URLs, methods, status codes and newer protocols. Chapter 1.5 maps the same layers to front-end, back-end and full stack roles, using the MERN stack as one example. Chapter 1.6 closes with VS Code, Git and browser consoles, the tools that edit, version and inspect the running system. Each chapter uses the previous one's picture, so the unit reads as one request path from click to database and back.

chapters.idea: A web page starts when a browser turns a URL into an IP address through DNS, then opens a connection and asks a server for a resource.
chapters.depth: Internet vs World Wide Web; packets, IP addresses and routers; DNS (Domain Name System) as a distributed name-to-address database. Cover URL parts: scheme, host, port, path, query and fragment. DNS hierarchy: resolver, root, top-level domain (TLD), authoritative server; A, AAAA, CNAME and MX records; TTL (time to live) and caching. HTTP uses port 80; HTTPS uses port 443. Follow one URL end to end: resolve host, TCP connect, send HTTP request, receive response, render. Mention that DNS answers are cached and can change.

figure.aria: Browser asks a resolver; the resolver walks root, TLD and authoritative servers, then returns 203.0.113.10 with TTL 300 s.

chapters.example: A browser opens https://shop.example.com:443/items?id=7. The resolver asks the root, the .com TLD and the authoritative server. The authoritative answer is A 203.0.113.10 with TTL 300 s. State the host, port, path and query. How long may a cache keep the answer? Which TCP port does the browser use after DNS? Answer: host shop.example.com; port 443; path /items; query id=7; cache up to 300 s; TCP port 443.
chapters.trap: A cached DNS answer skips root, TLD and authoritative servers until TTL expires. Port 443 is HTTPS; port 80 is HTTP.
chapters.leave: Packet-level routing, TLS handshake details and DNS server administration are not taught here; TLS appears only as the lock behind HTTPS in 1.4.

chapters.idea: A web system is split into client, server and data tiers so each part can be built, scaled and replaced on its own.
chapters.depth: Two-tier (client and database/server) and three-tier (presentation, business logic, data) models; n-tier or multi-tier as the general name. The client sends a request; the web tier accepts and routes; the application tier runs logic; the data tier stores state. Load balancer, cache and middleware positions. Stateless request handling and why sessions need shared storage. Cloud models named only as Infrastructure as a Service, Platform as a Service and Software as a Service; deployment details are in Unit 6. Use a request path: browser → load balancer → app server → database → back.

figure.title: Three-tier request path
figure.aria: Browser reaches a load balancer at 20 requests per second; it splits 10 requests per second to each of two app servers, both query one database.

chapters.example: An exam portal has 600 students. Each student sends 20 requests in the first 10 minutes (600 s). Find the average request rate. Each app server handles 15 requests/s. How many app servers are needed at that average? Average rate = 600 × 20 ÷ 600 = 20 requests/s. Servers needed = ⌈20 ÷ 15⌉ = 2. Each server gets 10 requests/s.
chapters.trap: A tier is a logical duty, not one machine. One physical server can host web and app tiers in a small app; a three-tier design can still run on three virtual machines or many containers.
chapters.prereq: 1.1: URL, DNS and the first client-server request.
chapters.leave: HTTP message details to 1.4; browser and server internals to 1.3; cloud deployment and CI/CD to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The browser renders and runs client code; the web server answers static requests or forwards dynamic ones; the application server runs business logic.
chapters.depth: Browser parts: rendering engine, JavaScript engine, network stack, storage and same-origin policy. Web server (Apache, Nginx) serves files, handles TLS and acts as reverse proxy. Application server (Tomcat, Express on Node.js) runs dynamic handlers and talks to databases. Static vs dynamic request; ports: 80 and 443 public, 3000 and 8080 internal in examples. Middleware as code between request and handler. Request lifecycle: accept, route, process, respond, log. Some syllabi call the application server the middleware host.

figure.title: Serving static and dynamic requests
figure.aria: Browser sends 1,000 requests per minute to a web server; 700 per minute go to static files, while 300 per minute go to an app server that queries a database.

chapters.example: Nginx receives 1,000 requests/min. 70% are static and 30% are proxied to Express. Find static and dynamic requests per minute and per second. Express handles 25 requests/s. Is it enough? Static = 0.70 × 1,000 = 700 requests/min = 11.7 requests/s. Dynamic = 0.30 × 1,000 = 300 requests/min = 5 requests/s. Yes, 5 requests/s is below 25 requests/s.
chapters.trap: The web server and application server are roles, not always separate machines. A Node.js process can serve static files and run app code; Nginx may sit in front as a reverse proxy.
chapters.leave: DOM and JavaScript details to Unit 3; Express routing and middleware code to Unit 6; TLS handshake to 1.4 only as HTTPS.

chapters.idea: HTTP is a stateless request-response protocol; HTTPS is HTTP carried inside TLS, and methods plus status codes carry the action and result.
chapters.depth: URL syntax recap; request line, headers, blank line, body; response status line, headers, body. Methods GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS; safe and idempotent properties. Status classes 1xx to 5xx and common codes 200, 201, 204, 301, 304, 400, 401, 403, 404, 500. HTTP/1.1 persistent connections; HTTP/2 multiplexing over one connection; overview of HTTP/3 over QUIC, a UDP-based transport (only a few universities teach HTTP/3 here). HTTPS uses TLS (Transport Layer Security) on port 443. WebSockets, a persistent two-way connection, and WebRTC, peer-to-peer media and data, are alternatives for live traffic (only a few universities teach these here).

figure.aria: Client sends GET, POST and DELETE; server replies 200 with 84 bytes, 201 Created and 204 No Content.

chapters.example: A client sends GET /items/7?expand=price HTTP/1.1 to api.example.com on port 443. The server returns 200 OK with Content-Type application/json and Content-Length 84. Then POST /items returns 201 Created, and DELETE /items/7 returns 204 No Content. Classify the three status codes, state whether GET is safe and idempotent, and give the body length of the GET response in bytes. Answer: 200, 201 and 204 are 2xx success; 204 has no body; GET is safe and idempotent; body length is 84 bytes.
chapters.trap: GET is safe and idempotent; PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is neither. A 404 means the resource is not found; a 500 means the server failed, not the client.
chapters.prereq: 1.1 for URL and DNS; 1.2 for client-server exchange.
chapters.leave: HTML forms and GET/POST form handling to Unit 2 and Unit 4; REST API design and JSON CRUD to Unit 6; TLS cryptography is not derived here.

chapters.idea: Front end, back end and database are roles in one request path; a full stack developer can work across them, and MERN is one JavaScript-based stack.
chapters.depth: Front end: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, UI framework, accessibility and browser performance. Back end: server language, routing, business logic, authentication and data access. Database: store and query. DevOps as build, test, deploy and monitor support (named here, taught in Unit 6). Full stack role combines front-end, back-end and data skills. MERN means MongoDB, Express, React and Node.js: React UI, Express REST API, Node runtime, MongoDB documents. Compare with PHP/MySQL or Java/Spring stacks. Request flow: React event → fetch JSON → Express route → MongoDB query → JSON response → UI update.

figure.aria: Stack from React UI at top through Express and Node.js to MongoDB at bottom, labelled with 12 KB response, 8 requests per second peak, 40 requests per second max and 250 products.

chapters.example: A MERN product page loads 20 products, each 0.6 KB of JSON. MongoDB stores 250 products. Express handles up to 40 requests/s; peak traffic is 8 requests/s. Find the JSON size, the spare capacity and the layer that owns a product document. JSON size = 20 × 0.6 KB = 12 KB. Spare capacity = 40 − 8 = 32 requests/s, or 5 times the peak. The product document is owned by MongoDB; React renders it and Express returns JSON.
chapters.trap: MERN is not a requirement for full stack work. Node.js is a runtime, not a framework; Express is the web framework. MongoDB stores documents, not tables.
chapters.prereq: 1.2 and 1.3 for tiers and servers; 1.4 for HTTP methods and status codes.
chapters.leave: React component details to Unit 5; Node, Express, MongoDB queries and authentication to Unit 6; deployment and DevOps practice to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Developer tools close the edit-run-inspect loop: VS Code edits, Git records versions, and browser consoles show what the page and network actually did.
chapters.depth: VS Code: editor, file explorer, integrated terminal, extensions, breakpoints and debug console. Git: repository, working tree, staging area, commit, branch, merge, remote, push and pull; .gitignore. Browser DevTools: Elements for DOM and CSS, Console for JavaScript errors and logs, Network for request URL, method, status, size and time, Application for storage and cookies. Read a request's status and transferred size. Local testing with console and breakpoints; deployment handoff is named and left to Unit 6. Commit is local; push uploads.

figure.title: Edit to inspect loop
figure.aria: Five-step flow from VS Code edit to Git stage, local commit, remote push and browser DevTools check with 34 KB transferred and one 404.

chapters.example: A page loads index.html 4 KB, app.css 12 KB and app.js 30 KB. app.css is in browser cache; the other two are downloaded. Git status shows modified app.css and new logo.svg. DevTools Console shows 404 for /favicon.ico. Find transferred bytes, the files to stage, and whether commit uploads. Transferred = 4 KB + 30 KB = 34 KB; cached CSS contributes 0 bytes. Stage 2 files. Commit is local; push is needed to upload.
chapters.trap: git commit saves to the local repository only; it does not upload. Browser cache can make Network show 0 bytes or from cache for a file, so transferred size is not total page weight.
chapters.prereq: 1.3 for browser and server roles; 1.4 for HTTP status and headers seen in Network.
chapters.leave: Git branching strategy, CI/CD and cloud deployment to Unit 6; full DOM debugging to Unit 3.
